cards.title: Mission purpose
cards.summary: Start with a useful outcome. The spacecraft is a means to answer a question or serve people.
cards.example: Our scenario asks for flood observations that reach emergency responders while they are still useful.
cards.impact: A sharp image delivered too late may not satisfy the mission. Design for the people using the data.
cards.source_label: NASA: Design and Develop Science Missions, slides 10-15

cards.title: Science requirements
cards.summary: Turn the goal into checks: what to observe, how well, how often, and when the result must arrive.
cards.example: A teaching scenario could require six useful observations before a delivery deadline. These targets are game assumptions.
cards.impact: Requiring finer detail can demand a different instrument and a larger resource budget.
cards.source_label: NASA: Design and Develop Science Missions, slides 18-19

cards.title: Spacecraft & instruments
cards.summary: The instrument makes the measurement. The spacecraft supplies power, pointing, computing, storage, and communications.
cards.example: A new imaging sensor still needs a stable pointing system and somewhere to store its observations.
cards.impact: Adding a capable sensor can increase science value, mass, cost, power demand, and data production together.
cards.source_label: NASA: science mission segments and design

cards.title: Mass & launch capacity
cards.summary: Include the whole spacecraft in its mass budget. A launcher must carry that mass to the chosen destination orbit.
cards.example: In a game example, 110 kg of hardware cannot use a launch option rated for 100 kg to that orbit.
cards.impact: A larger battery may solve an energy problem but require a heavier, more costly launch option.
cards.source_label: NASA: mission design and launch segment

cards.title: Power versus energy
cards.summary: Power (W) is the rate of energy use. Battery energy (Wh) determines how long a load can run without generation.
cards.example: A 20 W load uses 10 Wh in half an hour. This simple example ignores real battery losses and reserves.
cards.impact: Solar panels need sunlight. During eclipse, a larger battery helps endurance but adds mass and cost.

cards.title: Orbit & coverage
cards.summary: Altitude and inclination influence what a satellite can see and when it returns. Earth rotates beneath its orbit.
cards.example: An orbit that never passes near the target region cannot satisfy that region's observation goal.
cards.impact: Changing the orbit also changes observation timing, eclipses, ground contacts, and launch compatibility.
cards.source_label: NASA Earth Observatory: Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits

cards.title: Communications & data
cards.summary: Observations first occupy onboard storage. A downlink transfers them during usable ground-station contacts.
cards.example: In a simplified example, 2 MB/s for a 60-second contact transfers up to 120 MB before overheads.
cards.impact: More sensor data can overflow storage. A faster radio can help but also consumes power and budget.

cards.title: Budget & lifetime
cards.summary: A mission must support development, launch, and operations. A longer service period needs resources beyond the initial build.
cards.example: A teaching budget includes ground-station access and mission operations as well as the satellite and launch.
cards.impact: A cheaper component may free budget elsewhere. Cost alone does not determine whether the mission succeeds.
cards.source_label: NASA: overall mission concept and implementation

cards.title: Four mission segments
cards.summary: Launch gets hardware to space; the space segment measures; the ground segment receives; users turn results into knowledge or action.
cards.example: Our rocket, satellite, ground station, and flood-response team form one connected mission.
cards.impact: Improving only the satellite cannot fix an unavailable ground station or a missed user deadline.
cards.source_label: NASA: Design and Develop Science Missions, slide 8

cards.title: Verification & trade-offs
cards.summary: Decide how each requirement will be checked before building. Compare alternatives, then investigate why a check fails.
cards.example: Check payload mass against launch capacity and compare power demand with generation and stored energy.
cards.impact: Fixing one constraint may worsen another. Recheck the complete design after a change.
cards.source_label: NASA: Design and Develop Science Missions, slide 19
